The arm is the narrower of two exits: if the receiver is not a class the builtin cannot be statically identified at all and `_UNSUPPORTED_MANIFEST_VALUE` is returned, which raises upstream rather than recording a guess. R5 `isinstance(value, BuiltinFunctionType)` encodes a builtin as a `module:qualname` identity. Invalidated if builtins acquired a hashable implementation, or if a builtin's identity string stopped uniquely determining its behaviour.

R5 `isinstance(value, list)` is the list-constant arm, structurally parallel to the tuple arm above but a separate carrier: a list and a tuple with identical contents encode under different keys (`{"list": ...}` versus `{"tuple": ...}`) so that a literal changing carrier changes the manifest hash. It applies the same all-or-nothing unsupported propagation. Invalidated if the two carriers were ever collapsed into one encoding, which would make a real code change invisible.

R5 `isinstance(value, set)` inside the set-constant arm selects WHICH of the two set carriers is being encoded, choosing the `"set"` or `"frozenset"` key. It matters because a mutable set and a frozenset with equal contents are different constants in the source, and encoding both identically would let a `set` literal be edited to a `frozenset` without changing the manifest hash -- exactly the code drift the resume-trust manifest exists to detect. Invalidated if the distinction stopped being semantically meaningful in the hashed constants.

R5 `isinstance(value, (set, frozenset))` is the set-constant arm. Its distinguishing job is DETERMINISM: set iteration order is not stable across interpreter runs, so the normalized elements are sorted by canonical JSON before encoding. Without that sort the manifest hash for identical code would differ between runs and every resume would be reported as untrusted. The two set carriers share the arm because they share the sorting treatment, and are then told apart on line 169. Invalidated if the canonical-JSON sort key were removed or made non-total.

R5 `isinstance(value, dict)` is the dict-constant arm. Keys and values are normalized independently and the resulting pairs sorted by canonical JSON, because dict constants may be built from unordered sources and the encoding must be order-independent for the hash to be stable. It also propagates unsupported keys OR values, so a dict with one unencodable member fails loudly rather than being partially hashed. Invalidated if the pair sort were removed, which would reintroduce order-dependence into the manifest hash.

R5 `isinstance(value, bytes)` encodes a bytes constant as hex. It is required because bytes are not JSON-encodable at all; without this arm a bytes literal would fall through to `_UNSUPPORTED_MANIFEST_VALUE` and `_normalize_code_constant` would raise FrameworkBugError, making any function with a bytes constant unhashable and therefore unresumable. Hex is chosen over a text decode because it is total -- arbitrary bytes have no guaranteed text form. Invalidated if a lossy encoding were substituted, which would let two different byte strings hash alike.

R5 `isinstance(value, re.Pattern)` reifies a compiled regex constant into its pattern string and flags. This is load-bearing for the manifest's purpose: a compiled pattern is an opaque object whose identity says nothing about its content, so without unpacking it an edit to a validation regex would leave the manifest hash unchanged and a resumed run would trust code that had actually changed. Invalidated if `flags` stopped being part of the encoding, since the same pattern text under different flags matches differently.

R5 `isinstance(value, complex)` encodes a complex constant as its real/imaginary pair. complex is not JSON-encodable, so without this arm the constant would reach `_UNSUPPORTED_MANIFEST_VALUE` and raise. Splitting into two floats is the total, lossless form. Invalidated if complex constants stopped occurring in hashed code, at which point the arm would be dead rather than wrong.

R5 `isinstance(value, (str, int, float, bool))` is the JSON-primitive passthrough arm, returning the value unchanged. Its placement is the substantive part: it sits BELOW the bytes, regex, complex and slice arms so those richer types are reified first, and bool is named explicitly alongside int even though bool subclasses int, because both are JSON primitives that encode directly and no separate treatment is needed. Invalidated if any primitive acquired a required encoding wrapper -- for example if float NaN needed rejecting here, as it is elsewhere in the contracts layer.

contracts/runtime_val_manifest.py:R6:_re: R6 `except TypeError: namespace = {}` around `vars(owner)` in `_resolve_static_attribute`. The plan's default for this file's R6 sites is F, and this one is recorded as a deliberate exception with the reasoning stated for adjudication. `vars()` is DOCUMENTED to raise TypeError exactly when an object has no `__dict__`, so the except clause here is Python's sanctioned capability test, not an error being swallowed: both outcomes -- 'no instance dict' and 'name not in the instance dict' -- converge on the same next step, `_static_class_attribute(type(owner), name)`, so no information is lost and no failure is hidden.
